1374, a charter of the Koriatovych princes
The old town stands on a rocky island that the Smotrych canyon wraps almost all the way round. Only a narrow neck of land leads in, and that is where the castle rises.
After the Battle of Blue Waters in 1362, Podillia passed to the Lithuanian princes Koriatovych. Kamianets became their main seat.
In 1374 the Koriatovych princes granted the town Magdeburg rights. Ruthenians, Armenians, Poles and Jews lived side by side here, each community with its own churches.
A small town on the upper Smotrych, among the hills of the Tovtry.
In the second half of the 14th century the Koriatovych princes held a castle here, one of the first in Podillia. Later Kamianets, further down the river, took the lead.
The Golden Horde, then Lithuania after 1362
A town on the steep left bank of the Dniester, the centre of the land the chronicle calls Ponyzzia.
In the chalk cliff above the river, monks cut a cave monastery: cells and a church carved straight into the rock.
In 1255 the chronicle mentions the Horde's baskak Milei here. After 1362 the land passed to Lithuania, and Bakota gave way to Kamianets.
The Principality of Moldavia, from the second half of the 14th century
The fortress stands on the rocky right bank of the Dniester, by the old crossing between Podillia and Moldavia.

Its stone walls were raised under the Galician princes. In the second half of the 14th century Khotyn passed to the Principality of Moldavia, and from here the Moldavian rulers guarded their northern border.
1408, a charter of Prince Alexander the Good
The town grew on the high bank of the Prut, by a ford on the trade road.
Nearby stood the fortress of Tsetsyno, guarding the Prut valley.
In 1408 Chernivtsi was first recorded, in a charter of the Moldavian prince Alexander the Good, as a customs post for the merchants of Lviv.
The land of Galicia, from the second half of the 14th century the Kingdom of Poland
The castle stands on a hill above the spot where the Hnizna flows into the Seret.
The chronicle mentions Terebovlia in 1097: Vasylko Rostyslavych ruled here and was blinded after the Council of Liubech.
In the 14th century the land passed to the Kingdom of Poland, and in 1389 the town received Magdeburg rights.
